topics.title: What is the IASC?
topics.plain: The Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) is where the big humanitarian organizations agree how to work together. It is a forum, not an aid agency: it does not run field operations itself.
topics.detail: The IASC is the longest-standing and highest-level humanitarian coordination forum of the UN system. It was established in response to UN General Assembly Resolution 46/182 (adopted on 19 December 1991); the IASC Membership page dates the Committee's establishment to June 1992. The 2025–26 UN Handbook describes 19 Principals of UN and non-UN entities. The IASC is chaired by the Emergency Relief Coordinator (ERC).
topics.technical: Keep the chronology precise: Resolution 46/182 was adopted on 19 December 1991; the IASC Membership page gives June 1992 as the Committee's establishment date. Resolution 48/57 (1994) is cited as reaffirming the IASC's role as the primary mechanism for inter-agency coordination. The 2025–26 UN Handbook describes 19 Principals and says its information is accurate as at 1 July 2025.
points: A forum, not an operational agency
Chaired by the Emergency Relief Coordinator
topics.caveat: Do not collapse the date of Resolution 46/182 (1991) and the Committee's establishment date (June 1992) into one event. The IASC Membership page was not retrievable in this review; verify subsequent changes directly with the Secretariat.
followups: What does the IASC do and not do?
How do the Principals, Deputies Group, EDG, OPAG and Secretariat relate?

topics.title: What the IASC does — and does not do
topics.plain: It helps organizations agree on rules, priorities and joint responses. It does not hand out aid itself; its members do that.
topics.detail: The Overview page sets out four functions: (1) formulate humanitarian policy and guidance; (2) agree strategic priorities for the sector; (3) coordinate collective response to crises; (4) advance protection, accountability and principled action. What it does not do: run field operations or deliver aid directly. The Secretariat does not set policy either; it follows through on the Principals' decisions.
topics.technical: The four-function list is the Overview page's own summary; its source table does not cite a specific source for it, so treat the wording as secondary synthesis. The 'does not deliver aid' point is stated on the page and is consistent with the Secretariat's description of the IASC as a coordination forum.
topics.caveat: The four-function list is the explainer's own synthesis (no specific citation on the page).

topics.title: Who participates: members and standing invitees
topics.plain: Twelve UN bodies are members and seven others are permanently invited. In practice they sit at the same table.
topics.detail: The 2025–26 UN Handbook describes 19 Principals from UN and non-UN entities. It distinguishes full members from standing invitees and notes that NGO consortia ICVA, InterAction and SCHR are invited on a permanent basis. The IASC Membership page provides the Secretariat's own directory and should be checked for later changes.
topics.technical: The Overview page's displayed directory groups 12 organizations as members and seven as standing invitees. The 2025–26 UN Handbook reports 19 Principals, and states that its information is accurate as at 1 July 2025. Its membership narrative names OHCHR among standing invitees while its full-member roster also includes OHCHR; the assistant therefore flags the category rather than silently resolving the discrepancy.
points: 7 standing invitees (incl. Red Cross/Red Crescent, NGO consortia, World Bank, IDP Special Rapporteur)
No practical distinction between the two
topics.caveat: Membership and participation categories can change. The IASC Membership page could not be retrieved during this review. Confirm the current roster and OHCHR's formal category with the Secretariat before external use.

topics.title: Humanitarian principles
topics.plain: Four ideas guide all humanitarian work: help people because they suffer, help by need alone, don't take sides, and stay free of political or military agendas.
topics.detail: Humanity: human suffering must be addressed wherever it is found; the purpose is to protect life and health and ensure respect for human beings. Impartiality: action on the basis of need alone, priority to the most urgent cases, without discrimination. Neutrality: not taking sides in hostilities or engaging in controversies of a political, racial, religious or ideological nature. Independence: autonomy from the political, economic, military or other objectives of any actor.
topics.technical: The Overview page uses OCHA's standard formulation as used across UN humanitarian guidance. Humanity, neutrality and impartiality were set out in General Assembly Resolution 46/182; independence was added later by the General Assembly — that history is general knowledge (Tier 4) and is not stated on either page.
topics.caveat: No URL is given on the page for the OCHA formulation; none is invented here.
followups: How does Defend relate to the principles?

topics.title: How the IASC works: its structure
topics.plain: The IASC Principals provide collective leadership. The 2025–26 UN Handbook identifies three core subsidiary bodies: the Deputies Group, EDG and OPAG. Technical structures are time-bound and reviewed; the Secretariat supports deliberations and follow-up.
topics.detail: The 2025–26 UN Handbook describes the IASC Principals, supported by three core subsidiary bodies: the Deputies Group, the Emergency Directors Group (EDG) and the Operational Policy and Advocacy Group (OPAG). The technical structures created for specific workstreams are time-bound and regularly reviewed. The Handbook lists five entities associated with the IASC.
topics.technical: The Deputies Group provides dialogue and decision-making on strategic issues tasked by the Principals. The EDG advises and follows up on urgent collective operational action, system-wide resource mobilization and targeted field support. OPAG drives normative and strategic policy work on system-wide matters with a direct bearing on humanitarian operations. The five associated entities listed in the 2025–26 Handbook are the Inter-Agency Humanitarian Evaluation Steering Group, Global Cluster Coordination Group, Humanitarian Programme Cycle Steering Group, Reference Group on Gender and Humanitarian Action, and Reference Group on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support.
points: Principals → Deputies Group, EDG and OPAG
Technical structures are time-bound; five associated entities are listed in the 2025–26 UN Handbook
The Secretariat supports deliberations, follow-up and connectivity
topics.caveat: The 2025–26 UN Handbook states that its information is accurate as at 1 July 2025. It is a dated reference, not a live 2026 organigram. Technical structures are time-bound and regularly reviewed.

topics.title: What the Secretariat does
topics.plain: The Secretariat is the support team. It doesn't make policy; it helps make sure the Principals' decisions get acted on and keeps the different groups linked up.
topics.detail: The IASC Secretariat supports the Principals' deliberations, helps ensure decisions are followed through and builds connectivity across the IASC's formal structures and associated entities. It does not replace the mandates or accountability of participating organizations.
topics.technical: The Secretariat sits within OCHA's support architecture and provides connective and follow-up functions across the Principals, Deputies Group, EDG, OPAG and associated entities. Refer to the current Secretariat description before making claims about staffing, internal reporting or detailed responsibilities.
points: Builds connectivity across the Deputies Group, EDG, OPAG, time-bound technical structures and associated entities
topics.caveat: Do not describe the Secretariat as the policy-making authority or as an operational agency delivering humanitarian assistance.
followups: How do the Principals, Deputies Group, EDG and OPAG relate?

topics.title: Global vs country coordination
topics.plain: The Overview page explains global coordination (the IASC and its bodies). Country-level coordination is led by Humanitarian Coordinators and Humanitarian Country Teams, which the Reset page refers to but neither page describes in detail.
topics.detail: Global: the IASC Principals and their subsidiary bodies agree policy and priorities (Overview page). Country: the Reset page refers to Humanitarian Coordinators (HCs), Humanitarian Country Teams (HCTs), ERC–HC compacts, clusters and HNRPs — for example, 100% ERC–HC compacts (from 70% in 2024) and 79% of operations starting or completing cluster simplification. Neither page sets out the formal country-level architecture or how HCs are appointed.
topics.technical: Anything beyond the HC/HCT/cluster terms used on the Reset page — e.g. cluster lead agency roles or HC appointment procedures — would be Tier 4 general knowledge here and is not presented as sourced.
points: Global: Principals, Deputies Group, EDG, OPAG and time-bound technical structures
Country: HCs, HCTs, clusters and HNRPs (as named in the Reset source material)
The pages do not provide a complete formal country architecture
topics.caveat: This is a gap in the available sources, not a full answer. For country-level arrangements, consult current IASC guidance directly.
followups: How do the Principals, Deputies Group, EDG and OPAG relate?

topics.title: The Humanitarian Reset in two minutes
topics.plain: The Humanitarian Reset is the IASC's reform effort, adopted in February 2025. A draft stocktake from October 2026 says progress is real but uneven, and that results for people's lives have not yet been assessed.
topics.detail: Adopted in February 2025. The Reset is organized around Define, Deliver, Devolve and Defend. The accessible October Stocktake introduction reports 100M people with collective results, including 40M with life-saving support. Deliver separately reports 66M of 148M targeted reached, including 41M in the most severe locations across 24 operations. The exact 8 October revision cited by the website is not available in the review archive; source-version and calculation differences remain open.
topics.technical: Keep four measures separate: 100M collective results; 40M with life-saving support in the introduction; 66M reached of 148M targeted; and 41M of those reached in the most severe locations. The 41M share is reported as 63% in accessible October source copies, while rounded 41M/66M values yield approximately 62%. The website's cited 8 October data record states 62%; its exact file is unavailable for verification.
points: Four Ds: Define, Deliver, Devolve, Defend
Outcomes for people not yet assessed
topics.caveat: Both October source documents are drafts pending clearance. The page is an independent explainer. Reported implementation and reach do not establish outcomes or causality.
followups: Outcomes vs implementation — what's the evidence?

topics.title: The four Ds
topics.plain: Define: focus on the worst needs. Deliver: do the job more simply and fund it jointly. Devolve: give local organizations more say and money. Defend: stand up for humanitarian rules and staff.
topics.detail: Define — response concentrating where needs are most severe; more focused prioritization and slightly shorter planning. Deliver — 66M of 148M targeted reached; coordination simplified; pooled funds expanded; cash growing but short of targets. Devolve — local participation broadening; access to resources and decisions has further to go; some indicators fell. Defend — reported qualitatively: collective advocacy and humanitarian diplomacy, IHL and human rights, GBV response and PSEAH, standing with frontline colleagues in Sudan, OPT, DRC and Ukraine.
topics.technical: Define and Deliver carry most quantitative indicators; Devolve mixes allocations, governance and perception-survey data; Defend has no quantitative indicators in the Stocktake, and none are created here. The Four Ds Explorer lays these out side by side.
points: Deliver: reach, simpler coordination, pooled funds
topics.caveat: All figures are draft. Defend is qualitative only.
followups: Deliver — what does it show and not prove?

topics.title: Define: progress
topics.plain: Help is going more to the worst-hit places, plans are a bit quicker to make, and more plans say how aid will hand over to others.
topics.detail: The site-cited 8 October data record reports 62% of people assisted in severity 4–5 areas (36% in 2024, 43% in 2025). The accessible four-page October Stocktake draft and 17-slide presentation report 63% for 2026. 75% (15 of 20) 2026 HNRPs include steps toward responsible transition. GHO 2026 is 41% funded ($14.49bn of $35.07bn, end September); the hyper-prioritized plan is 55% funded ($13.63bn of $24.94bn). Median HPC time is 171 days, 11 days above the 160-day end-2027 target.
topics.technical: The exact 8 October revision cited for 62% was not available in the review archive. Accessible October source copies report 63%; the rounded 41M/66M ratio is approximately 62%, but unrounded counts are not supplied. The accessible four-page draft presents 17%, 40% and 75% as a transition-planning comparison; the implementation brief classifies the earlier values as cluster-plan measures. Do not present either series as fully reconciled without plan-level data.
points: Severity 4–5 reach: 62% in the site-cited 8 October record; 63% in accessible October copies
GHO funding: $14.49bn of $35.07bn raised; hyper-prioritized plan: $13.63bn of $24.94bn
HPC median: 171 days; end-2027 target: 160 days
topics.caveat: Source-version and methodology checks remain open. A smaller appeal footprint is a change in planning arrangements, not evidence that humanitarian needs have fallen. Serious protection risks may also exist in severity 3 locations.
followups: Why do accessible copies report 63% while the site-cited record says 62%?
Is the transition series a trend?
Deliver — what does it show and not prove?

topics.title: Deliver: what it shows and what it doesn't prove
topics.plain: About 66 million of 148 million targeted people got some help; pooled funds grew a lot; coordination got simpler. That shows activity, not yet whether lives improved.
topics.detail: By October 2026, 66M of 148M people targeted (45%) had been reached with some form of assistance and protection. Of those reached, 41M were in locations with the most severe needs across 24 operations. Accessible draft sources report 63% for the 41M share; the rounded values 41M/66M equal approximately 62%. The site-cited 8 October revision records 62%. CBPF contributions are $4.53bn as of 2 October in the site-cited revision and nearly $4.49bn at end-September in accessible October copies. 79% of operations had started or completed cluster simplification.
topics.technical: The introduction separately reports 100M people with collective results, including 40M with life-saving support; its methodology and overlap with the 66M Deliver measure are not set out. Do not equate the 40M with the 41M severe-location subset. Contributions are not disbursements. 'Started or completed' is not the same as 79% completed. The accessible source files report $702M (32% of CBPF funding) in CVA allocations; this is not the same denominator as CVA as a share of total humanitarian funding.
points: 41M in the most severe locations across 24 operations; 63% in accessible source copies
$4.53bn site-cited CBPF figure at 2 October vs nearly $4.49bn in accessible end-September sources
79% started or completed cluster simplification — not 79% completed
topics.caveat: Reach, allocation and process measures do not prove quality, sufficiency, sustained outcomes or causality. The 8 October Stocktake file cited by the site was not available for direct verification.
followups: Outcomes vs implementation — what's the evidence?

topics.title: Devolve: local leadership and resources
topics.plain: Local groups are taking part more, but how much money they get depends on what you count, and listening to community feedback dropped.
topics.detail: The site-cited 8 October version reports a 2026 local/national CBPF allocation share of 55% excluding US Award Tranche I and 20% including it. The accessible four-page Stocktake draft and presentation report 53% outside the initial US Award, comprising 40% direct and 13% indirect; the presentation separately reports 55% for 2025. The one-page summary identifies 14% of HCT seats held by local and national organizations. The 2026 WLO/WRO figure is 5% through 11 September (partial year).
topics.technical: The 2026 allocation figures are not a like-for-like trend; the exact 8 October source file and underlying allocation register were not available for this review. The HCT Perception Survey is preliminary, and respondents are not representative of all humanitarian actors or affected people. 56% perceive more inclusive coordination; 26% consider financial, operational and compliance risks equitably shared. Representation and allocation do not by themselves establish authority.
points: 55% excluding / 20% including US Award Tranche I in the site-cited 8 October record
53% outside the initial US Award in accessible October copies (40% direct + 13% indirect)
14% of HCT seats held by local and national organizations in the one-page draft summary
56% perceive greater inclusion; 26% consider risks equitably shared (preliminary survey)
topics.caveat: Do not combine 55%, 20% and 53% into one trend. Keep the US Award inclusion rule, direct/indirect definition, reporting date and source version next to every figure. 2026 data are subject to verification in H1 2027.

topics.title: Defend
topics.plain: Defend is about standing up for humanitarian rules and staff under pressure. The Stocktake describes it in words, not numbers.
topics.detail: The Stocktake says that in highly politicized crises, including Sudan, OPT, DRC and Ukraine, 'the IASC has stood visibly and consistently with frontline colleagues.' Collective advocacy covers principled humanitarian action and consistent application of IHL and international human rights law (by the ERC, Principals and HCs/HCTs); the life-saving nature of GBV response and risk mitigation; and PSEAH, kept distinct from and complementary to efforts on conflict-related sexual violence. Further work will document implementation of the Principals' humanitarian diplomacy recommendation.
topics.technical: No quantitative indicators are reported for Defend, so none are charted or invented here. Any 'progress score' for Defend would be fabricated.
points: IHL, human rights, GBV, PSEAH advocacy
Named contexts: Sudan, OPT, DRC, Ukraine
topics.caveat: Qualitative evidence only. Absence of numbers is not absence of activity — nor evidence of impact.

topics.title: Outcomes vs implementation
topics.plain: The Stocktake mostly measures what has been done (plans, funds, reach), not whether people are better off. It says so itself.
topics.detail: The Stocktake's introduction: 'progress remains uneven and the IASC is yet to assess outcomes of the Humanitarian Reset for the lives of vulnerable people.' Most indicators are inputs (funding), processes (planning time, cluster simplification), outputs (allocations) or reach (66M). None, on its own, establishes an attributable outcome or that the Reset caused a change.
topics.technical: Classify each figure before interpreting it: GHO funding and CBPF = inputs; HPC days, cluster simplification, compacts = process; allocations and CERF windows = outputs; people reached = reach; Perception Survey = perception. Outcome evidence (e.g. changes in mortality, protection or wellbeing attributable to the Reset) is absent from both source documents.
points: Stocktake itself says outcomes not yet assessed
Most figures are inputs, process, outputs or reach
followups: Deliver — what does it show and not prove?

topics.title: What's underway and what's next
topics.plain: Next steps: keep prioritizing, simplify further, strengthen accountability and get resources closer to the front lines. Several workstreams are still ongoing.
topics.detail: Next-phase priorities: continued prioritization; simpler ways of working; stronger accountability; greater proximity of resources to the front lines. HWG workstreams reported completed: simplified clusters, area-based coordination, tracking Reset progress (HCT Perception Survey), complementarity (adopted June 2026). Ongoing: HPC simplification, responsible use of AI, scaling cash, climate-sensitive anticipatory Reset, data collaboration, community consultations.
topics.technical: Workstream statuses come from presentation slide 13. 'Completed' means the workstream was reported complete, not that roll-out is finished (e.g. 79% of operations started or completed cluster simplification). Milestone statuses are recomputed against today's date in the Milestones view.
topics.caveat: Statuses are as reported in draft documents; check milestones against today's date.
followups: Outcomes vs implementation — what's the evidence?

topics.title: Key caveats when reading the Stocktake
topics.plain: Read every figure with its date, its base and its definition — and remember the documents are drafts.
topics.detail: Key qualifications: the 100M collective-results measure (including 40M with life-saving support) is not the same as 66M reached of 148M targeted; 41M of the 66M are in the most severe locations. Accessible October sources report 63% for this 41M share, while the site-cited 8 October version records 62%. CBPF values differ by cut-off date. Local allocation shares vary by inclusion of US Award Tranche I and by calculation basis. Transition-plan comparability is unresolved. The Perception Survey is preliminary; Defend is qualitative; outputs and reach are not outcomes.
topics.technical: The exact 8 October Stocktake file referenced by the site was not available for direct verification in this review. Use the discrepancy ledger for source-by-source values and do not silently choose, average or infer causality.
topics.caveat: All underlying October 2026 IASC source materials remain drafts pending clearance. This is an independent explainer, not an official IASC publication.

topics.title: Finding the original sources
topics.plain: The two original Reset documents are drafts and are not publicly available. The Reset page is the reproduction you can read.
topics.detail: The IASC Stocktake (draft, 8 October 2026 revision) and the presentation (draft, 17 slides) are both marked 'pending clearance · not yet published'. No public URL exists in this registry, and none is invented. Published, linkable sources in the registry: the EU statement of 27 October 2026 and UNDP's conversation with Tom Fletcher.
topics.technical: When an original becomes public, add its URL and change its status in registry.json; the drawer will link it automatically.
topics.caveat: Answers about Reset figures therefore rely on the secondary page, not the original documents.
followups: Find an official document or source.

indicators.caveat: This 40M figure is distinct from the 41M reported in Deliver as people reached in locations with the most severe needs. The sources do not establish whether the groups overlap.

indicators.title: People assisted who are in intersectoral severity 4–5 areas
indicators.definition: Share of people receiving assistance and protection who are in areas of intersectoral severity 4 and 5 (JIAF scale).
indicators.caveat: The website's cited 8 October revision records 62%, but that exact file was not available for this review. The accessible four-page October draft and 17-slide presentation both report 63%; neither provides unrounded underlying counts. The accessible documents reviewed do not support the previously listed 55% presentation value. Keep the version difference visible pending the exact 8 October file and calculation base.

indicators.title: 2026 HNRPs outlining steps towards responsible transition
indicators.definition: Humanitarian Needs and Response Plans with steps, milestones and timelines towards responsible transition.
indicators.caveat: The accessible four-page October draft says 75% (15 of 20) HNRPs in 2026, up from 40% in 2025 and 17% in 2024. The project implementation brief separately classifies the earlier 17% and 40% figures as cluster-plan measures. The underlying plan-level table is not supplied here; comparability of the three values must be verified before presenting them as a continuous trend.

indicators.title: Operations that have started or completed cluster simplification
indicators.definition: Operations that have started or completed simplification of cluster arrangements.
indicators.caveat: Started or completed, not 79% completed. No earlier figure is reported, so no trend is shown.

indicators.title: Median days to complete the Humanitarian Programme Cycle
indicators.definition: Median planning time for the Humanitarian Programme Cycle.
indicators.caveat: Down 8 days since 2024; 11 days above the 160-day target set for end-2027. The target is not an achieved result.

indicators.title: Funding raised against the GHO 2026
indicators.definition: Funds raised against total GHO 2026 requirements, from 61 Member States and public and private sources.
indicators.caveat: The hyper-prioritized plan is 55% funded ($13.63bn of $24.94bn); the two denominators differ.

indicators.title: Country-based pooled funds
indicators.definition: Contributions to OCHA country-based pooled funds; $3.75bn of the 2026 total is US awards.
indicators.caveat: The site-cited 8 October revision reports $4.53bn as of 2 October; the accessible four-page draft and 17-slide presentation report nearly $4.49bn at end-September. The different cut-off dates may matter, but the records do not prove the cause of the difference. Contributions are not disbursements.

indicators.title: Cash and voucher assistance share of total funding
indicators.definition: Cash and voucher assistance as a share of total funding. The source material describes an envisaged target of 35%; it separately reports a 2026 CBPF allocation of $702M (32% of CBPF funding).
indicators.caveat: Do not confuse CVA as a share of total humanitarian funding with CVA as a share of CBPF allocations. The 35% and 85% targets are described as envisaged, not achieved results.

indicators.title: Local and national share of 2026 pooled-fund allocations
indicators.denominator: Excluding | including US Award Tranche I
indicators.definition: Share of CBPF allocations to local and national actors, direct and indirect. Excluding US Award Tranche I: 55% ($182M), 44% direct. Including it: 20% ($409M).
indicators.caveat: The site-cited 8 October revision reports 55% excluding and 20% including US Award Tranche I as of 28 September. The accessible four-page draft and presentation separately report 53% outside the initial US Award (40% direct + 13% indirect); the accessible presentation reports 55% for 2025. These values have different versions, bases and/or periods and are not a continuous trend. 2026 data remain subject to verification in H1 2027.

indicators.title: HCT seats held by local and national organizations
indicators.denominator: Humanitarian Country Team seats; seat count not stated
indicators.definition: Share of HCT seats held by local and national organizations, described in the one-page Stocktake summary as the primary authority indicator.
indicators.caveat: Representation is not the same as decision-making authority, influence or control over resources. The source does not provide the underlying count or a disaggregated country roster.

indicators.title: Allocations to women-led and women's rights organizations
indicators.definition: Share of allocations to women-led and women's rights organizations against a 15% annual target.
indicators.caveat: Partial-year position; not comparable with full-year 2024 or 2025 results.

indicators.title: ERC–HC compacts
indicators.denominator: Number of ERC–HC compacts; count not stated
indicators.definition: Reported uptake of ERC–HC leadership accountability compacts.
indicators.caveat: A process/coverage measure of accountability arrangements; it does not establish the quality or effect of the compacts.

indicators.title: HNRP countries where HCTs regularly discuss feedback trends
indicators.definition: Humanitarian Country Teams that regularly discuss community feedback trends.
indicators.caveat: A decrease of 13 points. Not all Devolve indicators are improving.

indicators.title: Respondents who see coordination as more inclusive of local actors
indicators.definition: Perception Survey respondents perceiving coordination as more inclusive of local actors. 26% consider financial, operational and compliance risks equitably shared.
indicators.caveat: Perceptions of respondents; not representative of the wider humanitarian community. Delayed country responses may change the findings.

indicators.title: Respondents who consider financial, operational and compliance risks equitably shared
indicators.definition: Share of Perception Survey respondents who consider financial, operational and compliance risks equitably shared.
indicators.caveat: Perception Survey respondents are coordination actors, not a representative sample of all humanitarian actors or people affected by crises. Delayed country responses may change findings.

discrepancies.label: People assisted in severity 4–5 areas, 2026

values.value: 62% in the 8 October 2026 revision referenced by the website; exact file not available in the review archive
63% in the accessible four-page October Stocktake draft
63% in the accessible 17-slide October presentation

discrepancies.explanation: The site-cited 8 October revision records 62%, while the accessible four-page draft and 17-slide presentation both report 63%. Dividing rounded headline values 41M by 66M gives approximately 62%, but unrounded counts are not supplied. The accessible source copies reviewed do not support the previously listed 55% presentation value. The exact 8 October file and calculation base are required to resolve this.
discrepancies.do_not: Describe 62% as independently verified against the 8 October file, retain 55% as the presentation value without a supporting file, or substitute a derived percentage for the source-reported value.

discrepancies.label: 100M collective results, 40M life-saving support, 66M reached and 41M severe-location reach

values.value: Introduction: 100M collective results, including 40M with life-saving support
Deliver: 66M of 148M targeted reached; 41M of those in the most severe locations across 24 operations
Retains 100M / 40M and 66M / 41M framings; labels reach figures unreconciled
66M reached, including 41M in the most severe locations

discrepancies.explanation: These are not interchangeable measures. The accessible introduction describes 100M collective results including 40M with life-saving support. Deliver separately reports 66M reached out of 148M targeted, including 41M in the most severe locations. The sources do not specify the counting method or overlap for 100M, nor whether the 40M life-saving-support group overlaps with the 41M severe-location group.
discrepancies.do_not: Add the figures, equate 40M with 41M, or describe 100M as the same people-reached measure as 66M.

discrepancies.label: Country-based pooled funds, 2026

values.value: $4.53bn as of 2 October 2026 (8 October revision referenced by the site)
Nearly $4.49bn at end-September 2026
Nearly $4.49bn at end-September 2026

discrepancies.explanation: The reporting cut-off dates differ. The available records do not include the underlying contribution register needed to determine whether the difference is fully explained by timing. Contributions are not disbursements.
discrepancies.do_not: Describe the gap as verified growth, a correction or an accounting error without the underlying fund contribution records.

discrepancies.label: Local and national share of pooled-fund allocations

values.value: 55% excluding US Award Tranche I; 20% including it, as of 28 September 2026 (8 October revision referenced by the site)
53% outside the initial US Award, including 40% direct and 13% indirect
53% outside the initial US Award, including 40% direct and 13% indirect; 55% is the 2025 figure

discrepancies.explanation: The accessible draft and presentation report a 53% 2026 share outside the initial US Award, while the site-cited 8 October version records 55% excluding and 20% including US Award Tranche I. The presentation's 55% is separately a 2025 figure. Definitions, inclusion criteria and cut-offs must be reconciled against the exact 8 October file and underlying allocation data. 2026 values remain subject to verification in H1 2027.
discrepancies.do_not: Treat 55%, 20% and 53% as a single series, compare them as like-for-like trend values, or infer a change in authority from allocation shares alone.

discrepancies.label: Responsible transition planning, 2024–2026

values.value: 75% (15 of 20) 2026 HNRPs; draft text says up from 40% in 2025 and 17% in 2024
The site's implementation brief classifies the 17% and 40% earlier values as cluster-plan measures, separate from 2026 HNRPs

discrepancies.explanation: The accessible four-page draft's prose presents 17%, 40% and 75% as a transition-planning comparison. The implementation brief and current site notes classify the earlier 17% and 40% as cluster-plan measures. The plan-level source table is not available in the reviewed archive, so the measurement unit and comparability cannot be settled.
discrepancies.do_not: Draw one continuous trend or claim a 58-point improvement until the plan types and denominator for each year are confirmed.

discrepancies.label: Area-based coordination

values.value: 14 operations; seven country names are listed in the accessible four-page draft
Workstream reported as completed; not quantified on the slide

discrepancies.explanation: The accessible Stocktake gives a count of 14 operations but names seven in the list. The presentation reports the workstream as completed without quantifying it. Confirm whether the seven names are examples or the full list.
discrepancies.do_not: Infer that 14 is a complete country roster or that workstream completion means area-based coordination is operating everywhere.

discrepancies.label: Completed workstreams versus operation-level rollout

values.value: Simplified Clusters listed under workstreams completed
79% of operations had started or completed cluster simplification by October 2026

discrepancies.explanation: The presentation's 'completed' label refers to the workstream milestone; the Stocktake's 79% refers to operation-level rollout, combining operations that started or completed simplification. These statements describe different levels of completion.
discrepancies.do_not: Rewrite the 79% figure as '79% completed' or imply that every operation has completed simplification.

discrepancies.label: Defend evidence and measurement

values.value: Qualitative reporting; no numerical Defend indicator supplied

discrepancies.explanation: The accessible Stocktake describes advocacy, support for frontline leadership, protection, IHL/IHRL and PSEAH qualitatively. It does not supply a quantitative Defend score.
discrepancies.do_not: Invent a score, proxy KPI or numerical progress bar for Defend.

reading_rules.rule: The HCT Perception Survey reflects respondents' perceptions and cannot be treated as representative of the wider humanitarian community; it is preliminary (Sept 2026) and delayed responses may change it.
Defend is reported qualitatively. No quantitative Defend indicators exist in the sources, and none are created.
Outputs, milestones, allocations and reach do not by themselves establish attributable outcomes or causality. The Stocktake says outcomes for people have not yet been assessed.
Milestones are re-evaluated against today's date; past-due items without a record of completion are shown as 'past due — status unconfirmed', never in the future tense.
Both Reset source documents are drafts pending clearance. Appearing on a web page does not make a claim cleared or endorsed.

glossary.def: Inter-Agency Standing Committee — the primary global mechanism for inter-agency humanitarian coordination, established June 1992 following UNGA Resolution 46/182.
Emergency Relief Coordinator — chairs the IASC.

Executive heads of the IASC's participating UN and non-UN entities. The 2025–26 UN Handbook describes 19 Principals and identifies the Emergency Relief Coordinator as Chair; this is a dated reference.

Core IASC subsidiary body described in the 2025–26 UN Handbook. It advances strategic dialogue and decisions on issues tasked by the IASC Principals. Check the Secretariat's live description for subsequent changes.
Emergency Directors Group — chaired by OCHA's Director of Operations; current crises and urgent operational needs.

Operational Policy and Advocacy Group — one of the three core subsidiary bodies described in the 2025–26 UN Handbook; works on system-wide normative and strategic policy matters affecting humanitarian operations.

A term used in earlier IASC governance descriptions for technical expert groups. Do not present Results Groups as part of the current 2025–26 structure; technical structures are time-bound and reviewed.
A permanently invited participant (e.g. ICRC, IFRC, NGO consortia, World Bank). In practice no distinction is made from members.
The IASC's reform effort adopted in February 2025, organized around Define, Deliver, Devolve and Defend.
Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan — a country plan; 20 in the 2026 cycle per the Stocktake.
Humanitarian Programme Cycle — the collective planning cycle; median completion 171 days in 2026 against a 160-day end-2027 target.
Global Humanitarian Overview — the annual appeal; GHO 2026 required $35.07bn for 148M people.
Central Emergency Response Fund; the Stocktake cites its Rapid Response and Underfunded Emergencies windows.
Joint Intersectoral Analysis Framework scale: 1 Minimal, 2 Stress, 3 Severe, 4 Extreme, 5 Catastrophic.
Humanitarian Working Group — the body whose workstreams track Reset implementation, per the presentation.
Protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment — kept distinct from, and complementary to, efforts on conflict-related sexual violence.

lessons.title: The IASC in five minutes
steps: The IASC is a humanitarian coordination forum, not an operational agency delivering aid directly.
UNGA Resolution 46/182 was adopted on 19 December 1991; the IASC Membership page dates the Committee's establishment to June 1992.
The 2025–26 UN Handbook describes 19 Principals from UN and non-UN entities; membership categories and invitee status should be checked against the Secretariat's current directory.
The 2025–26 UN Handbook identifies the Deputies Group, EDG and OPAG as core subsidiary bodies; technical structures are time-bound and the Secretariat supports follow-up and connectivity.
Four humanitarian principles guide the work: humanity, impartiality, neutrality and independence.

check.q: Which statement about the IASC is supported by the sources?

options.text: It runs field operations in crisis countries.
options.why: The Overview page says the IASC itself does not run field operations; its members do.

options.text: It is a coordination forum chaired by the ERC.
options.why: Both the Overview page and the Secretariat describe it this way.

options.text: Standing invitees cannot take part in decisions.
options.why: The Secretariat says no distinction is made in practice between members and standing invitees.

lessons.title: How to read a stocktake figure
steps: Check the source version: the website cites an 8 October revision, while accessible October draft copies in the project archive report some different figures.
Find the denominator: 66M is out of 148M targeted, not out of everyone in need.
Find the definition: '79% started or completed' is not '79% completed'.
Find the source and its status: the October 2026 Stocktake and presentation are drafts pending clearance.
Ask what kind of figure it is: input, process, output, reach, perception — or outcome? Most are not outcomes.

check.q: 41M people were reached in the most severe locations. How does that relate to 66M reached?

options.text: 41M is a subset of the 66M; accessible October source copies report 63%, while rounded 41M/66M is approximately 62%.
options.why: The Stocktake describes 41M 'of them' in the most severe locations; the accessible draft reports 63%, but displayed headline values are rounded.

options.text: 41M is part of the 100M, so 66M is wrong.
options.why: 100M and 66M are different framings; neither cancels the other.

lessons.title: When two sources disagree
steps: The website's 8 October source record lists 62% of people assisted in severity 4–5 areas in 2026; accessible four-page Stocktake and 17-slide presentation copies report 63%.
The exact 8 October file and unrounded counts were not available in the review archive.
The honest response is to show the source-version difference and not substitute an unsupported 55% value.

check.q: Do the accessible October source copies and the website's cited 8 October record report exactly the same severity 4–5 share?

options.why: The accessible four-page draft and 17-slide presentation report 63%.

options.text: No — the site-cited 8 October record says 62%; accessible copies say 63%.
options.why: The exact 8 October source file and unrounded counts are unavailable for this review.

lessons.title: Humanitarian principles
steps: Humanity: address suffering wherever it is found.
Impartiality: act on need alone, most urgent first, without discrimination.
Neutrality: take no sides in hostilities or controversies.
Independence: stay autonomous from political, economic or military objectives.

check.q: Prioritizing assistance by need alone, without discrimination, describes which principle?

options.why: Neutrality is about not taking sides.
Impartiality means acting on the basis of need alone.
Independence is autonomy from other actors' objectives.

simulation.label: FICTIONAL LEARNING SCENARIO — NOT OPERATIONAL GUIDANCE
simulation.title: Coordination after a flood in fictional Rivarno
simulation.setting: Rivarno is an invented country. No real places, people, beneficiary data or operational procedures are used. All names and figures are invented for learning.
objectives: Weigh incomplete and conflicting information before acting.
Connect coordination choices to inclusion of local actors and to humanitarian principles.
Notice how early choices change what information becomes available later.
Explain your reasoning, not just your choice.
simulation.role_limits: You play a fictional inter-agency coordination officer supporting a fictional Humanitarian Country Team. You advise; you do not command agencies, allocate funds alone or speak for the HCT. Real decisions of this kind belong to accountable leadership following approved procedures.

steps.title: Day 3: two estimates, one missing voice
steps.prompt: Three days after flooding in Rivarno's (fictional) Lowmere district, two sector leads give you different severity estimates for the same area. A network of local NGOs says it was not consulted on either. You must recommend how the next 48 hours of coordination meetings run.
steps.uncertainty: Neither estimate states its method. You do not know whether the network's members have field data of their own.

choices.text: Adopt the higher estimate to be safe and move straight to planning.
choices.feedback: Speed matters, and erring high can protect people. But the method gap is untouched and the local network is still outside the room — both will resurface.

choices.text: Hold a short reconciliation session within 24 hours, with the local network invited.
choices.feedback: You trade a day for a shared baseline and a wider set of voices. The cost is real: a day's delay in a fast-moving situation.

choices.text: Let both estimates stand and plan on each in parallel.
choices.feedback: You avoid a confrontation now, but downstream plans will sit on two incompatible baselines.

steps.title: Day 5: new information arrives
steps.prompt: A fictional rapid assessment now suggests access to two villages is cut by a damaged bridge, and that women-headed households there are under-represented in both earlier estimates. A donor asks for a single headline number of 'people reached' by tomorrow.
steps.uncertainty: The assessment covers only part of the district. 'Reached' has not been defined between partners.

context_by_previous.a: Because planning started on the higher estimate, two partners already used it in their own reports.
context_by_previous.b: Because the local network joined, its members were the ones who flagged the bridge.
context_by_previous.c: Because two baselines are in circulation, partners disagree on which villages are 'covered'.

choices.text: Send the donor the largest available figure, labelled 'reached'.
choices.feedback: It satisfies the request but conflates targets, planned reach and actual reach — the same trap as treating 148M targeted as 148M helped.

choices.text: Send a range, define 'reached', state the period, and flag the access gap.
choices.feedback: Less tidy, more honest. A defined measure with a denominator and caveat is what makes a figure usable later.

choices.text: Decline to give any number until the full assessment is done.
choices.feedback: Accurate, but silence can push partners to fill the gap with their own, less careful numbers.

steps.title: Day 8: a principled tension
steps.prompt: A fictional local authority offers safe passage across the river — on condition that its own officials choose which households receive help first.
steps.uncertainty: You do not know how the authority would select households. Refusing may delay help to people cut off.

choices.feedback: Access is vital, but letting a party select recipients risks impartiality (need alone) and independence.

choices.text: Recommend the HCT negotiate access while keeping selection based on assessed need, and escalate through leadership.
choices.feedback: This keeps principles central and recognizes that the decision belongs to accountable leadership — at the cost of time and an uncertain negotiation.

choices.text: Refuse and wait for another route.
choices.feedback: Principled, but it may leave people without help for longer; exploring negotiation first is usually part of the trade-off.

rubric.label: Evidence use
rubric.question: Did you define measures, state periods and denominators, and show uncertainty?

rubric.label: Coordination
rubric.question: Did your choices keep partners on a shared picture?

rubric.label: Inclusion / participation
rubric.question: Were local actors and under-represented groups brought in?

rubric.label: Principles
rubric.question: Did you protect humanity, impartiality, neutrality and independence?

rubric.label: Risk / uncertainty
rubric.question: Did you name what you did not know and plan for it?

rubric.label: Reasoning
rubric.question: Could you explain the trade-off you accepted at each step?

pillars.title: Define
pillars.short: Concentrate response where needs are most severe; make planning more focused.
pillars.headline: Response is concentrating where needs are most severe
pillars.what: Prioritization and planning have become more focused, with some reduction in the time required for collective planning.
questions: Which source version supports 62% and which supports 63%?
Is a smaller appeal a sign of lower need, or of different planning?
Do the underlying plan-level records confirm the 17%, 40% and 75% comparison?
pillars.caveat: 'A smaller appeal footprint is a change in planning arrangements, rather than evidence of reduced needs.' Serious protection risks may also exist in severity 3 locations.

pillars.title: Deliver
pillars.short: Reach people through simpler coordination and expanded pooled funding.
pillars.headline: Coordinated action reached 66 million of the 148 million people targeted
pillars.what: Coordination arrangements are being streamlined, pooled funding has expanded and reported shares of cash assistance have increased.
questions: Is this an input, an output, reach — or an outcome?
What is the denominator and the cut-off date?
pillars.caveat: 'Operational contributions depend on award conditions, timely disbursement and access.' Reach is not proof of outcomes or causality.

pillars.title: Devolve
pillars.short: Broaden local participation and move resources and decisions closer to the front lines.
pillars.headline: Local participation is broadening; access to resources and decisions has further to go
pillars.what: Steps are being taken to broaden local actors' participation and strengthen country-level accountability, with further work needed on access to resources and decision-making.
areas: Pooled-fund allocations to local and national actors
questions: Is the US Award Tranche I counted?
Direct or indirect — and how is 'indirect' derived?
Is a partial year comparable with a full year?
pillars.caveat: 'These figures are not a like-to-like trend.' Perception Survey results cannot be treated as representative of the wider humanitarian community.

pillars.title: Defend
pillars.short: Stand with frontline colleagues and uphold principles, IHL and human rights under pressure.
pillars.headline: The IASC has stood visibly with frontline colleagues under sustained pressure on norms
pillars.what: Collective advocacy and humanitarian diplomacy have continued, alongside efforts to uphold protection, gender equality and PSEAH commitments.
areas: Principled action, IHL and international human rights law
Humanitarian diplomacy in politicized crises (Sudan, OPT, DRC, Ukraine)
questions: What kind of evidence is this — documented action, statements, or results?
What would a credible measure of Defend look like, and who would own it?
pillars.caveat: The Stocktake reports Defend progress qualitatively; it gives no quantitative indicators, so none are shown.

validation_flags: The exact Stocktake 8 October 2026 revision cited by the website is not available in the review archive; do not present its values as independently re-verified.
Accessible October source copies report 63% severity 4–5; the site-cited 8 October record says 62%; unrounded values and exact file are needed to reconcile.
Accessible October sources say 100M collective results including 40M life-saving support; Deliver separately says 66M reached including 41M in severe locations. Overlap is not defined.
Local allocation values 55% / 20% and 53% have different source versions and/or inclusion bases; do not trend them together.
The 2025–26 UN Handbook describes institutional structure as accurate at 1 July 2025; current IASC Secretariat pages should be rechecked when accessible.
All October 2026 IASC source documents in the reviewed archive are draft and pending clearance.
